name: Dutasteride
lead: Dutasteride, sold as Avodart among other brands, is an oral medication that inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). It is FDA-approved for symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and is used off-label for male pattern hair loss in most countries; it is approved for male androgenetic alopecia at 0.5 mg per day in South Korea (2009), Japan (2015) and Taiwan (2016), according to Wikipedia.[1][2]

Unlike finasteride, which inhibits the type II and III isoenzymes, dutasteride inhibits types I, II and III, and Wikipedia reports it can lower circulating DHT by up to 98 percent versus 65 to 70 percent for finasteride.[1] A phase III trial compared several dutasteride doses with finasteride and placebo in men with androgenetic alopecia, and a systematic review reported an efficacy ranking of dutasteride 0.5 mg above finasteride 1 mg.[3][4]

Reported adverse effects are mainly sexual (erectile dysfunction, reduced libido, ejaculation disorders) plus breast disorders; a 2019 meta-analysis found a 1.37-fold relative risk of sexual dysfunction with dutasteride that was not statistically significant, with limited trial data.[5][2] Its elimination half-life of about 4 to 5 weeks means it remains in the body for months after stopping.[1] It is contraindicated in pregnancy and carries an FDA warning relating to high-grade prostate cancer and PSA interpretation.[2][1]
infobox: Oral; topical and mesotherapy forms used off-label
Glaxo Wellcome (GSK); patented 1996 per Wikipedia (lead cites 1993)[1]

paras: Wikipedia states that several studies found dutasteride to induce regrowth in men more rapidly and to a greater extent than the highest approved finasteride dose, which it attributes to more complete inhibition of DHT production in follicles.[1] The drug is also used off-label for female pattern hair loss.[1] A review reports that clinicians increasingly use it and oral minoxidil off-label because only finasteride is FDA-approved for male alopecia among oral options.[3]

Because oral dutasteride may cause sexual and neurological side effects, a 2025 review describes efforts to develop topical and nanocarrier formulations aimed at follicles with less systemic uptake; on T Nation, users describe topical dutasteride and dutasteride mesotherapy as alternatives.[6][7]

The US label indicates dutasteride to improve symptoms and reduce the risk of acute urinary retention and BPH-related surgery in men with an enlarged prostate, alone or combined with tamsulosin, and states it is not approved for prevention of prostate cancer.[2] Trials include a 2002 study of 4,325 men and the CombAT study of dutasteride with tamsulosin.[8][9][10]

Wikipedia says dutasteride is sometimes used in transgender women's hormone therapy and is being investigated for premenstrual dysphoric disorder because it may block conversion of progesterone to allopregnanolone.[1]

In a 2006 randomised placebo-controlled study, dutasteride was compared with finasteride on the premise that dual 5-alpha-reductase inhibition matters in male pattern hair loss.[11] The 2014 phase III trial randomised men aged 20 to 50 to dutasteride (0.02, 0.1 or 0.5 mg), finasteride 1 mg or placebo.[4] Systematic reviews and a meta-analysis compare dutasteride and finasteride on hair regrowth and reversal of miniaturisation, in men and women, and a 2024 updated review covers dutasteride for androgenetic alopecia.[12][13][14]

A 2022 comparison review ranked probable efficacy as dutasteride 0.5 mg, finasteride 5 mg, minoxidil 5 mg, finasteride 1 mg, then minoxidil 0.25 mg.[3] A randomised placebo-controlled study tested microneedling plus topical dutasteride solution.[15]

For hair loss, human data include the 2006 and 2014 randomised comparisons with finasteride, a 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of dutasteride versus finasteride, a 2022 randomised trial of microneedling with topical dutasteride, and registered bioequivalence and post-marketing studies (for example a surveillance study of 712 patients with alopecia, NCT01004809, and a bioequivalence study of 0.1 mg capsules, NCT01929330).[11][4][12][15][16][17] Topical use is reviewed in a 2025 paper.[6]

For BPH and prostate cancer, major trials include the REDUCE trial in men aged 50 to 75 with elevated PSA, a 2002 study of 4,325 men, a 2004 study showing marked DHT suppression and the CombAT 2-year and 4-year results.[18][8][19][9][10] A 2019 meta-analysis of randomised trials of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors for hair loss included limited dutasteride data and said more trials are needed.[5] Grokipedia says REDUCE showed a 22.8 percent reduction in prostate cancer incidence with more high-grade tumors detected, a figure attributed to that AI-generated source.[20]

The label lists impotence, decreased libido, ejaculation disorders and breast disorders as the most common reactions.[2] In the largest BPH study of 6,729 men, Wikipedia reports erectile dysfunction in 9 percent (5.7 percent on placebo), decreased libido in 3.3 percent (1.6 percent) and enlarged breasts in 1.9 percent (1 percent).[1] The 2019 hair-loss meta-analysis found a non-significant increase for dutasteride, but noted that studies were limited.[5] A comparison review associates oral finasteride and dutasteride with sexual dysfunction and neuropsychiatric side effects.[3]

The FDA label states dutasteride reduces serum PSA by about 50 percent, that a confirmed PSA rise may signal prostate cancer, and that it may increase the risk of high-grade prostate cancer; Wikipedia notes the FDA added a boxed warning in 2011.[2][1] Women who are or may be pregnant should not handle the drug, which can cause genital abnormalities in male fetuses, and because of its long half-life donors should not give blood for at least six months after stopping.[2][1]

On T Nation, some users attribute lasting impotence or penile changes to dutasteride, including after topical or one-week use, and another poster reported breathlessness and palpitations after switching from finasteride; these are anecdotes, and the sources reviewed contain no controlled study of those outcomes.[21][22][23][24]

Dutasteride is a competitive, mechanism-based inhibitor of all three 5-alpha-reductase isoforms, with IC50 values of 3.9 nM for type I and 1.8 nM for type II.[1] Both dutasteride and finasteride lower prostate DHT by roughly 85 to 90 percent, where type II predominates, but dutasteride lowers circulating DHT further.[1] The enzyme inhibitors also block neurosteroid synthesis including allopregnanolone.[1] A 2018 review cited by Wikipedia found no consistent testosterone rise on initiating 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.[1]

Oral bioavailability is about 60 percent, peak levels occur in 2 to 3 hours, and the drug is metabolised by CYP3A4 to active metabolites.[1] The terminal half-life is about 4 to 5 weeks, steady state needs 5 to 6 months, and the drug can be detected for 4 to 6 months after stopping.[1][3]
Dutasteride is a 4-azasteroid and an analogue of finasteride in which the tert-butyl amide is replaced by a 2,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl group.[1]

Wikipedia says dutasteride was patented in 1996, described in the literature in 1997, FDA-approved for BPH in November 2001, and launched as Avodart in 2002; its patent expired in November 2015, after which generics became available.[1] South Korea approved it for hair loss in 2009, Japan in 2015 and Taiwan in 2016.[1]

subs.h: Use in hair-loss and looksmaxxing communities
paras: Community threads on tressless.com and r/tressless ask why dutasteride is not recommended first, compare it with finasteride, or ask whether to switch from dutasteride to finasteride.[25][26][27] On T Nation, users discuss topical dutasteride with RU58841 or CB-03-01 to control hair loss during testosterone therapy, claim topical dutasteride gives fewer sides than topical finasteride, and trade experiences about side effects and post-finasteride syndrome.[28][21][29]

timeline.event: FDA approves dutasteride for BPH; launched as Avodart in 2002.[1]
Phase III BPH study of 4,325 men published.[8]
Randomised study of dutasteride versus finasteride for male pattern hair loss published.[11]
South Korea approves dutasteride for hair loss.[1]
REDUCE prostate cancer trial published in NEJM.[18]
FDA boxed warning on high-grade prostate cancer risk.[1]
Phase III dose-ranging trial versus finasteride and placebo in androgenetic alopecia published.[4]
Japan approves for hair loss; US patent expires.[1]

lore.intro: In hair-loss communities dutasteride is discussed as the stronger alternative to finasteride, used orally, topically or by mesotherapy, with a parallel thread of side-effect reports.[25][26][28]

claims.claim: Dutasteride is stronger than finasteride and should be tried first
claims.believers: Posts ask why the community does not recommend it directly and describe it as the off-label darling for male pattern baldness.[26][30]
claims.experts: A phase III trial and review rankings place dutasteride 0.5 mg above finasteride 1 mg for hair outcomes, though it is approved for hair loss only in a few countries and trial data are limited.[4][3][1]

claims.claim: Topical dutasteride avoids the side effects of the oral drug
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said topical dutasteride gave him no sides unlike topical finasteride, though another reported penile shrinkage afterwards.[28][21]
claims.experts: A 2025 review says developing a safe and effective topical product is challenging and aims to limit systemic absorption; a poster notes some topical drug still reaches blood.[6][31]

claims.claim: Dutasteride can cause lasting impotence or hormonal damage
claims.believers: Users describe impotence continuing months after short use, or hard-flaccid symptoms and penile changes.[23][21][24]
claims.experts: Meta-analysis found no statistically significant increase for dutasteride in trials but too few studies; labels list sexual effects and the half-life is weeks.[5][2][1]

claims.claim: Dutasteride raises testosterone more than finasteride
claims.believers: A poster states it raises testosterone more and cites a PubMed link.[32]
claims.experts: A 2018 review summarised by Wikipedia found no consistent testosterone increase overall, with men of lower baseline testosterone showing an increase.[1]

claims.claim: Dutasteride microneedling or mesotherapy enhances results
claims.believers: Users report dutasteride mesotherapy as part of their hair protocol.[28]
claims.experts: A randomised placebo-controlled study of microneedling with topical dutasteride has been published.[15]
